reconcile.connective: JFB reads Mark's silence as confined to the road itself — the women told no bystander, yet still reached the disciples exactly as Matthew records.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses this in his 2006 Craig debate: "Did the women tell anyone or not? It depends which Gospel you read."

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: "Is There Historical Evidence for the Resurrection of Jesus?" (Craig–Ehrman debate)
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, in the Craig–Ehrman debate, "Is There Historical Evidence for the Resurrection of Jesus?" (College of the Holy Cross, March 28, 2006)

excerpts.excerpt_text: and did run to bring his disciples word--"Neither said they anything to any man [by the way]; for they were afraid" (Mar 16:8).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB directly pairs Matthew's 'ran to bring his disciples word' with Mark's 'said nothing to any man,' inserting the interpretive bracket '[by the way]' to confine the silence to the road so both reports stand.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), pp. 328-330
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact tension under 'Historical Discrepancies,' citing Ebrard's view that the women hastened back intending to tell the disciples but, finding them sunk in gloom, at first held back from fear of ridicule -- and offers the alternative that Mark and Matthew describe two different parties of women.

link.title: Is there a Bible contradiction in Mark 16:8?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of this exact verse, arguing the women's initial fearful silence (Mark) gave way to telling the disciples later that day (Matthew/Luke).
